sections.b: The Astronomical Book of 1 Enoch (chapters 72–82) is the oldest Jewish calendar text we have. The sun moves through six gates on the eastern horizon, thirty days in each, with a thirty-first day at the end of each quarter "because of its sign" (72:13). Twelve months of 30 days plus four added days make 364 days, exactly 52 weeks (72:32). The moon, with its 354-day year, falls behind by ten days a year and exactly one month in three years (74:13–14). The book blesses those who "do not sin as the sinners do in counting all their days" (82:4), and warns that people go wrong by leaving out the four added days (75:2; 82:5).

Jubilees turns Enoch's year into a command and condemns those who follow the moon (Jubilees 6:32–38). The Dead Sea Scrolls use it in calendar texts that track the twenty-four priestly divisions through six-year cycles (4Q319–4Q321), and a pesher on Habakkuk records that the Wicked Priest attacked the Teacher of Righteousness on the Teacher's Day of Atonement (1QpHab 11:4–8), a clash that makes sense only with two calendars. In this year Passover always falls on a Tuesday and the Day of Atonement on a Friday, and no feast falls on a Sabbath.

common: The 364-day calendar was kept by the Qumran community and is taught in 1 Enoch and Jubilees.
The Jerusalem temple and the later rabbis followed a moon-based year with added months.
uncommon: Annie Jaubert argued that Jesus ate the Last Supper on Tuesday evening by the 364-day calendar; most scholars are not persuaded.
Some scholars think the 364-day year was once the temple's own priestly calendar.

sections.b: In the Astronomical Book (1 Enoch 72–82) Enoch is a scribe who writes down what the angel Uriel shows him about the sun, moon, stars and winds (74:2), and hands his books to his son Methuselah to pass on "to the generations of the world" (82:1). This matches the hint in Genesis that Enoch lived 365 years, the days of a solar year (Genesis 5:23), and Jubilees' claim that he was the first to write down the signs of heaven (Jubilees 4:17–18). In 81:5–6 Enoch is given one more year on earth to teach his children before God takes him (Genesis 5:24).

common: The Astronomical Book is probably the oldest part of 1 Enoch.

sections.b: 1 Enoch never names a feast, but it insists that the lights mark "the feasts" (82:7; 82:9) and that people sin by miscounting the days (82:4–5). In the 364-day year that it teaches, and that Jubilees and the Qumran texts use, every feast falls on the same weekday every year: Passover on Tuesday, the Feast of Weeks on Sunday, the Day of Atonement on Friday. In a moon calendar, by contrast, Passover and Booths fall at the full moon (78:13; Leviticus 23:6; Leviticus 23:34).

sections.h: A year made of whole weeks
sections.b: 1 Enoch's 364-day year is exactly 52 weeks (72:32), and the book counts time in "Sabbaths," that is, weeks (79:2; 79:4). Because the year has whole weeks, no feast in it ever falls on a Sabbath, a feature its users seem to have valued.

The Astronomical Book is a long reading of Genesis 1:14–18. The lights rise and set "as the Lord commanded" (72:36), the sun "does not rest" (72:37), and everything keeps its order "until the new creation is made" (72:1). When people sin, the order seems to break (80:2–7), but the book never doubts that God made and rules the sky.

sections.h: Uriel and the officers of the stars
sections.b: In 1 Enoch 72–82 the angel Uriel, "God is my light," is set by "the Lord of glory" over all the lights of the sky (75:3; 82:7–8). Under him the stars are organized like an army: four leaders of the seasons, twelve leaders of the months, and "heads of thousands" over the days, all with names (82:9–20). The Bible pictures the stars as "the whole army of the sky" (Deuteronomy 4:19) and angels over fire and waters (Revelation 14:18; Revelation 16:5), but names no angel over the lights.

uncommon: The Ethiopian Orthodox Church honors Uriel as an archangel with feast days; the Catholic Church discourages naming angels other than Michael, Gabriel and Raphael.

sections.b: 1 Enoch shows that three 364-day years are exactly one month longer than three moon years (74:13–14). The Qumran calendar scrolls build on this with six-year cycles in which the twenty-four priestly divisions rotate exactly 13 times (6 × 52 = 312 weeks = 13 × 24), so that each division's week of service can be fixed in advance.

In 1 Enoch 81 Enoch reads "the book of the heavenly tablets," with "all the deeds of human beings" to the last generation (81:1–2), and blesses the one who dies with "no book of wrongdoing written about him" (81:4). Jubilees often speaks of laws and events written on the heavenly tablets. The Bible knows heavenly books of names, days and deeds (Exodus 32:32; Psalm 139:16; Daniel 7:10; Revelation 20:12).
1 Enoch's Astronomical Book opens by saying that the laws of the lights hold "until the new creation is made that will last forever" (72:1), echoing Isaiah's new heavens and new earth.

1 Enoch 80 foretells that "in the days of the sinners the years will be shortened," rain will stop, the moon will change its order and stars will stray (80:2–6), and people will treat the stars as gods (80:7). The Gospels also speak of shortened days and signs in sun, moon and stars (Mark 13:20–25).

Enoch calls his astronomical books "wisdom" given to Methuselah and his children for all generations, "beyond their thoughts," sweeter than fine food (82:2–3). Wisdom here includes knowing God's order in the sky.

1 Enoch 77:3 places "the garden of righteousness" in the third part of the north, beyond the dark seas, while Genesis puts the garden "in Eden, toward the east" (Genesis 2:8). Other parts of 1 Enoch return to this garden (32:3; 60:8; 70:3).

1 Enoch 82:16–19 describes spring and summer by their signs: the wheat harvest and roses, then heat, ripe fruit, mating flocks and the winepress. The pattern fits the farming year of Judea, as do the Bible's harvest feasts.

In 1 Enoch 80:6 "many of the leaders of the stars will stray from the command." The picture of stars as servants who can disobey links the Astronomical Book with the punished stars of the Book of the Watchers (18:13–16; 21:3–6) and the "wandering stars" of Jude 13.

Four Aramaic manuscripts of the Astronomical Book were found in Qumran Cave 4 (4Q208–4Q211). The oldest, 4Q208, is dated by its handwriting to about 200 BC. They show the book was once much longer than the Ethiopic: they hold a day-by-day table of sun and moon that the Ge'ez summarizes in chapters 73–74, and material on the seasons that the Ge'ez lost after 82:20.
1 Enoch warns that when the sky's order is hidden from sinners they will "treat the stars as gods" (80:7), agreeing with the Torah's ban on worshiping "the whole army of the sky" (Deuteronomy 4:19).
